title: An Artificial System Can Still Run Without Still Being Qualified to Continue
summary: Artificial continuity depends on technical function, valid data, permissions, interfaces, dependencies, and governance; execution capability is not the same as authority to carry reality.
shortAnswer: Artificial continuity depends on technical function, valid data, permissions, interfaces, dependencies, and governance; execution capability is not the same as authority to carry reality.
displayQuestion: An Artificial System Can Still Run Without Still Being Qualified to Continue

blocks.text: Artificial-system failure does not begin only when hardware or software stops. A machine can be healthy, a program can execute, and a service can remain reachable while the system is no longer fit to carry the same real-world responsibility. Data can be outdated, permissions can change, interfaces can lose compatibility, and dependent services can stop satisfying their original assumptions.

Book III separates two questions: “can the system do this?” and “should it still do this now?” The first concerns execution capability. The second concerns whether the evidence remains valid, the permission still exists, the risk is acceptable, and responsibility is clear. A plausible output does not automatically grant an agent the authority to inject that output into real decisions.

That is why artificial maintenance cannot be reduced to uptime. Continuity also needs restricted modes, read-only states, pause, degradation, and exit. When a source becomes invalid, the affected judgment should be able to stop rather than forcing every feature to behave as if the system were complete. Knowing when not to continue is part of reliability.

More dependencies can increase capability while making continuity more relational. Databases, identity systems, networks, external interfaces, models, storage, and permissions can each change the conditions of the final result. Maintenance must therefore cover not just components but dependency relationships and fallback paths.

The deeper issue is correspondence with reality. An artificial system can calculate an outdated world with perfect internal consistency. A lack of internal errors does not prove that its inputs still match current conditions. Sources, rules, authorization, and observed outcomes must therefore be recalibrated; technical stability without reality calibration can simply extend a mismatch.

blocks.heading: Key judgment
blocks.statement: Execution capability answers “can it be done?”; carrying authority answers “should it be done now, on what basis, and under whose responsibility?”

blocks.question: If a system still produces outputs after its data, permissions, or real-world conditions have changed, is it preserving continuity or amplifying mismatch?
